items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: When you got to Paris... you also were jamming with people like Django Reinhardt. Right.

ctx.x: Can you just tell us a few things about Django and your impressions of him when you first came across him?

Not much. There wasn’t much to know about Django. He was very quiet. He had very little to say. That’s being redundant, isn’t it? [Berger laughs.] But anyway, he was also maybe a little on the shy side, and maybe that was more because being around American musicians and not speaking English, and we not speaking French very well, you know, that probably was part of his feeling. But I couldn’t tell you very much about him, no more than you would read about him, maybe, certainly not as much, because the people that…
known him much better than I did have written rather widely about him, like, for instance, the Charles Delaunay’s book, you know, on Django Reinhardt. But I didn’t know him well.

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I met John Reinhardt and Stephen Corpelli

ctx.x: Well, it was. I was tremendously impressed. I had heard so much about of Paris, and I started playing at this club, which was a late hour club; you know, you played until the last spending customer left, and that could be 5 or 6 o'clock in the morning, and maybe even later.
You know? But I did like Paris; I met John Reinhardt and Stephen Corpelli, and Alex Combelle and oh, Phil Brun and Arthur Briggs -- people like that.
